standard.title: How authors organise ideas
standard.description: analyse how authors organise ideas to develop and shape meaning
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify how authors structure texts and organise information to achieve purpose (AC9E7LY04). They have not yet analysed the specific organisational logics — proposition and support, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution — and how these structures shape the meaning a text produces.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse how authors organise ideas — using structures such as proposition/support, cause/effect and compare/contrast — to develop and shape meaning.

nodes.label: Idea organisation structures
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the organisational structure a text uses (e.g. proposition and support, cause and effect, compare and contrast, problem and solution) and explain how that structure shapes the text's meaning.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the organisational structure used in one provided text (e.g. a news article or argument) and explain how that structure shapes what the reader understands from the text.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how texts structured according to proposition and support, cause and effect, compare and contrast, or problem and solution each shape meaning differently; identify examples of each structure and explain the effect the structural choice has on a reader.
wider: Compare how a news article and an academic essay organise the same information differently and analyse how the structural difference shapes the meaning and credibility each text produces

Investigate how a problem-solution structure can be used persuasively — examining what is at stake in the problem framing and whether the proposed solution addresses all aspects of the defined problem
Analyse how the organisation of a webpage (e.g. a news site or advocacy site) uses non-linear structure and shapes meaning differently from a linearly structured print text

response_modes.reason: Students may know proposition-support from English but not recognise the same organisational logic appearing as cause-effect in other subjects or as problem-solution in design. Encountering the structures across multiple text types builds a transferable analytical vocabulary.

success_criteria: Names the organisational structure used in a text (proposition/support, cause/effect, compare/contrast, or problem/solution).
Explains how that structural choice shapes what the reader understands or is persuaded of.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to analyse how organisational choices shape and limit meaning — a task that requires being able to name and classify the organisational structure in question. Students who cannot identify whether a text uses cause-effect or problem-solution logic cannot analyse the meaning implications of that structural choice.

nodes.label: How organisation shapes and limits meaning
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how an author's organisational choices not only develop meaning but also constrain what meanings are possible — examining what organisational choices include, exclude and imply.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one way in which the organisational structure of a text shapes or limits the meaning it can produce — what it makes visible and what it makes invisible.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how authors organise ideas to develop and shape meaning across a range of text types; discuss the effectiveness of different organisational approaches for their stated purpose; examine how texts that organise ideas around a problem can frame the solution in ways that limit alternatives.
wider: Rewrite a section of a text using a different organisational logic (e.g. change from cause-effect to problem-solution) and analyse how the structural change shapes the meaning produced

Investigate how the organisational structure of a web page shapes user behaviour and meaning-making differently from printed text — and what ideological or commercial purposes that structure might serve

Analyse how a First Nations text organises knowledge according to principles that differ from Western logical structures (e.g. relationally, through narrative, through Country) and how this creates different kinds of meaning

response_modes.reason: The insight that organisational choices are not neutral — that how ideas are arranged shapes what meaning is produced — is a critical thinking integration point. It requires students to hold both the content and the structural logic simultaneously and see that the structure is itself an argument.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The critical analysis of organisational logic — especially the concept that structure shapes and limits meaning — is a transferable critical thinking skill with applications across English, HASS and media literacy. Rich comparative material (webpages, advocacy sites, alternative organisational traditions) supports deep analytical work.
success_criteria: Identifies the organisational structure of a text and analyses how it develops the author's intended meaning.
Identifies at least one way the structural choice shapes or limits what meanings the text can produce.
